### Downloads

| file | for |
|---|---|
| `aht-<version>-macos-universal.zip` | macOS 13+, Apple Silicon and Intel (`aht.app`: menu bar tray + core + watcher + badge tool) |
| `aht-setup-<version>-windows-x64.exe` | **Windows 11 on x64: the installer** (for you only, no admin prompt; Start menu entry, Settings > Apps to remove it) |
| `aht-setup-<version>-windows-arm64.exe` | Windows 11 on ARM: the installer (native build) |
| `aht-<version>-windows-x64.zip` | Windows 11 on x64 without installing (`aht.exe`, `aht-tray.exe` and their `_internal` folder; run `aht install`) |
| `aht-<version>-windows-arm64.zip` | the same for Windows 11 on ARM |
| `SHA256SUMS.txt` | checksums of the above |

Package managers: `brew install --cask havurgiray/tap/aht` (macOS), `winget install havurgiray.aht` (Windows, the installer above), `scoop install aht` (Windows, after adding the `havurgiray/scoop-bucket` bucket). Linux installs from the checkout (`linux/install.sh`).

### In short

- **Five agents:** Switch Agent adds Antigravity and Mistral Vibe, and **Hand Back** returns the work to the session it came from, with a catch-up.
- **Your other machines:** Hand Over and Take Back now work between Mac, Windows and Linux, at any path.  New: **Bring Here** and **Send Back**, **Pick Up** and **Leave a Note**, **Watch** a machine, **search everywhere**, and another agent on the other machine.
- **Windows:** a PC asks your Mac and Linux machines without an ssh server of its own, and with OpenSSH Server it can also be handed projects, kept in sync with, keep backups and take a Send Back.
- **Sync safety:** Keep in sync looks before it overwrites; a handover cut off halfway settles itself; **Release** frees a project from a machine that is gone.
- **File copy:** rsync is now optional; aht copies files itself over ssh.
- **Permissions:** the agent that continues the work starts in the level of the session it continues, never higher.
- **Masking:** keys are masked whole, and the search index is rebuilt once.

### Before you upgrade

- **Windows, if you used aht before 0.14.0:** Windows Security took the small script older versions started the watcher with at sign-in for malware and removed it, so the watcher may not have started at sign-in since.  0.14.0 starts it without any script; run the installer, or `aht install` once, to set it up again.
- **Scoop:** run `aht install` once after `scoop update aht` to 0.14.0.  The hook and the sign-in entry then go through Scoop's `current` folder, so they keep working after later updates.
- **Mac, a path with `&` or `<`:** a watched folder, a home folder or an app location whose path holds `&` or `<` now gives valid LaunchAgents (the watcher, the notices, start at login).  Before, launchd would not load them, so the watcher silently did not run.  After the upgrade, Settings > This Mac > *Reinstall or Update aht…* rewrites them (`aht install` in a terminal rewrites the watcher's and the notices').

### Agents

**Five agents, and Hand Back.**
- Switch Agent now also offers Antigravity (the `agy` command) and Mistral Vibe (the `vibe` command), next to Claude Code, Codex and Kimi Code; the menu lists the ones installed.
- The agent that takes over goes on in a new session that reads a summary of where things stood, or in its own latest session in the project, which reads only a catch-up of what happened since (`aht switch <path> --to X --resume`).  *Summary Only* (`--brief-only`) writes the summary and opens nothing; who has the project stays as it was.
- While another agent has a project, a line under it says so (*Codex has had this project since 14:10, taken over from Claude Code*), with *Hand Back…*, also the first item under Switch Agent.  The first agent's own session opens again and reads what happened meanwhile: the other agents' exchanges, the to-dos still open, the files changed (from git) and the commits made (`aht switch <path> --back`).  When that session is gone, a new one reads the full summary and the catch-up; when aht cannot read what the other agent did, the catch-up says the files may differ all the same.
- Tokens: Hand Back to Claude Code, or going on in Claude Code's own session, costs no tokens until you type: aht's hook gives the session its catch-up as it opens.  Switching to, or handing back to, Codex, Kimi Code, Antigravity or Mistral Vibe is one turn of that agent; writing a summary costs nothing.
- A Claude session that another agent took the work over from, resumed by hand, is told in one line that the files may have changed and where the summary is.
- Each hand-off leaves a record next to its summary in the project's `.aht/handover/`, and `aht relays <path>` lists who handed the work to whom and when.
- Summaries now also hold the state of git, the files a Codex patch changed and Codex's plan, and say how many Codex sessions aht cannot read (Codex's newer storage).  aht reads the sessions of Codex 0.164, which keeps them in a new format, as well as older ones; Codex's background service no longer counts as an open Codex session.
- Kimi Code goes on in its own session too; when Kimi does not take the catch-up there, a new session reads the full summary, and aht says so.
- aht reads Antigravity's conversations, so it can continue one and catch it up, and Mistral Vibe's sessions (those of Vibe 3) the same way, in search, summaries and catch-ups as well, without ever changing them.

**Another agent on the other machine.**
- Hand Over and Bring Here can now go on in Codex, Kimi Code, Antigravity or Mistral Vibe (`aht handover <path> --agent codex`, `aht bring … --agent codex`; in the dialogs, *Agent there*).  Claude Code's history travels as always; the other agent starts a new session that reads a summary as its first turn, in the permission level of the session it continues (one turn: it uses tokens, and the dialog says so).
- Its state on the board comes from its tmux window: *working*, *quiet for 6 min*, *exited*, and a notice says *api on box went quiet*.  `aht attach <path> --peek` prints the last lines of the session there.
- Take Back waits while it runs; `--stop` ends it only after 2 minutes without output and once its own message ends its turn, by its quit keys (refusing with *quiet for only 1 min* or *its last turn is still open*), and never closes a window whose agent runs.  The quit keys are not yet confirmed with every agent version.
- On the way back, Take Back and Send Back bring a catch-up of what it did, made and masked over there, to the Claude Code session that left, which hears it once from aht's hook when you resume it.
- The other machine stays awake while that window wrote output in the last 10 minutes.

### Your other machines

**Between Mac, Windows and Linux, at any path.**
- Hand Over and Take Back now work from a Windows PC too, with your Mac and Linux machines, and a project may sit at another path on each machine.
- New: *Bring Here* (`aht bring <path there> --from <machine>`; *Projects → Bring Here → From …*) runs on the machine that gets the work.  It fetches a project with Claude Code's history and opens its session in a terminal, where nothing runs until you type; the project's home notes that it is away.  *Send Back* (`aht send-back <path>`) returns the work: the home plans it as Take Back would, and sets aside what it replaces.  Both need aht installed on the project's home.
- So a PC works on a Mac's project without the Mac having to reach it: the Mac shows "On pc since 14:10 (brought there from pc). Send it back from pc." with *Release…*, and the PC's tray lists *Projects brought here* with *Send Back…*.
- Where projects go is a rule per machine (`aht remote paths <machine> [--same | --home | --add HERE THERE | --remove HERE]`; *Machines → Folders there → Change…* in aht's window): a machine added now gets them at the same place below its home folder, and one set up before keeps the same paths when your home folder's path exists there.  A project outside every rule is refused, with the line that fixes it.
- Claude Code's history is filed under the folder's path there; /rewind's snapshots go only on an unchanged path; other agents' histories stay, and the session gets a summary.
- Before anything moves, aht refuses a folder there that holds something else, and names the other disk cannot hold (Windows' reserved names and characters, two names that differ only in case, links your account cannot make there), with *Leave Them Out…* (`handover_excludes`).
- On the way back, a file that changed only in its line endings is not taken, one whose line endings flipped as a whole gets back the ones it left with, executable marks survive a round trip through a PC, and a file whose name Windows cannot hold is kept aside under a safe name.
- A session aht starts gets `core.filemode=false` on a PC (and `core.autocrlf=true` for a project from a PC whose git converts line endings) through `GIT_CONFIG_*` in its environment; `.git/config` is never edited.  For a git project without a `.gitattributes` that crosses to or from Windows, the dry run suggests lines for one, which aht never writes.

**Pick Up and Leave a Note:** go on with a project's work on another machine, in any agent, and give it back later.  Only the context moves; git moves the files, and each machine keeps its own copy of the project, at any path.
- *Machines → Pick Up from box…* (`aht pickup <path> --from box`) brings a summary of the latest session in the project on box, made and masked there, and says what git still has to do ("On box: branch main, 1 commit not pushed, 1 file not committed. Commit and push there, then pull here.").  *Open in* starts the agent you choose with it (one turn: uses tokens); *Copy the Start Line* writes it and opens nothing.
- aht finds the project there by its id, else by its git origin and first commit, its path or its place in the home folder, and when two folders could be it, it lists both instead of guessing.
- *Leave a Note on box…* (`aht leave-note <path> --on box`) puts a summary of the work here into the project's `.aht/handover/` on box; aht only adds files there, nothing runs there and it costs no tokens.  When the work comes back the way it went, the summary is a catch-up for the session it left, which goes on in its own session; while work picked up from box is here, *Hand Back to box…* leaves such a note there.
- A note that arrives gives a notice, a line under the project with *Read the Note…*, and one line to the next Claude session there.
- A Windows PC starts every exchange: Pick Up from the Mac, then Leave a Note on it before you go.  In Search, a result from another machine offers *Continue Here…*, which picks that session up here.

**Watch a machine and search everywhere.**
- A *Watch* switch for each machine (`aht remote watch <machine> [--off]`): aht asks it every 2 minutes and tells you when a session there waits for you or is done, also when it holds no project of yours.  The Machines tab says when aht last heard from each one.
- Once you added a machine, every notice names its machine ("api on box waits for you"), and a notice from another machine reaches the phone only once: not when aht there sends it already.  A machine that holds a project and has not answered for 10 minutes gives one notice ("box has not answered since 15:20. The work on api there may have stopped (asleep, off or offline).").  In Sessions, a machine that does not answer keeps the sessions it had, greyed, "as of 11:40".
- *Also on my other machines* in Search (`aht search <words> --everywhere`): each machine searches its own index, read only, and its results come labelled with its name.  aht builds no index there and keeps nothing of the results.

**Handovers that were cut off.**
- When the link drops or the computer sleeps during a handover, aht now finds out at its next check whether the session on the other machine started, and finishes the handover or undoes it: "Handover of api to box finished: the session there runs (the link had dropped at 01:02)", or "The handover of api to box did not finish. The project stays here; nothing runs there".
- It counts as finished whenever something happened there: a session runs there, the copy there changed, "the conversation went on there", or "the session there started, and has ended since"; "did not finish" only when nothing happened there, so work done there is never dropped.  A handover that fails before the session starts says "did not finish" at once.  Folders taken along with `--include` come back at Take Back here too.
- The Mac app and aht's window show such a project with *Check Now*, which asks the other machine at once, and *Release…*; until it is settled, Continue Session, Switch Agent, Hand Over and Keep in sync wait.  The Mac menu lists such projects, and a click on the notice opens the project.  A session started in the project meanwhile is warned.  On Linux the tray shows these notices, and with `notify_phone` they reach the phone too.

**Release.**
- `aht reclaim <path> --release` (dry run first, then `--apply`) lets a project count as here again when the other machine is gone or does not answer: the files here stay as they are, the copy there is left alone, and the work done there stays there ("The work done on box since 14:10 stays on box. It does not come here. What stays there: 3 files and the conversation.").  It says nothing stays behind only when neither the files nor the conversation changed there.  It is offered after an hour without an answer.
- When the project is kept in sync with that machine, Release pauses Keep in sync, so no sync overwrites the copy left there; it stays paused until you turn it back on (*Turn Sync Back On…* in the Mac app and in aht's window, or `aht mirror <path> --on --to box`), or until a later Hand Over to that machine, which sets the released copy aside there first.
- The Mac app has *Release…* next to *Take Back…* for any handed-over project; aht's window has *More → Release from <machine>…*.  `aht remote remove`, and *Remove…* in the Machines tab, now say why a machine that still holds a project is not removed and point to Release.  The next session in a released project is told once that the work done there did not come here.  Take Back now refuses a saved list of what left that belongs to another handover attempt, and points to Release.

**Backups on another machine.**
- Each computer now gets a folder of its own there, named by a random id, so two computers of one name no longer share a folder.  Copying only adds: a backup there is removed only after this computer pruned it, and at least 3 per project always stay.  The copies aht makes before it rewrites a history go there too and are never removed there.
- New: `aht backup --offsite-list` lists every computer's folder there, and `aht backup --fetch-offsite [--from ID|NAME]` fetches from one; a fetch adds what is missing and never overwrites (a same-named backup of another size arrives as `<stamp>-from-<name>.zip`).  A backup that cannot be put in place is named, the others still arrive, and the command then ends with exit code 1.
- An older aht's folder named after this computer is taken over only when everything in it is here too, and goes once nothing is left in it; otherwise it stays, *Copy Now* says so, and *Fetch Backups From…* can bring its backups here.  The Mac app and aht's window have Settings → Backups on another machine with *Copy Now* and *Fetch Backups From…*.

**The other machine.**
- While the agent works on a project handed over to a Mac or Linux machine, aht keeps that machine from sleeping (`caffeinate`; `systemd-inhibit`, or GNOME's own inhibitor where ssh sessions may not use it; `handover_keep_awake`, on by default).  A closed lid still sleeps.  *Check* says whether it works there.
- The copy of aht placed on the other machine is now named after its checksum (`~/.aht/remote/aht-<checksum>.py`; the newest 3 stay, the old `aht.py` goes) and is sent only when it is missing, not with every look at that machine's sessions.  What a session waits for is masked before it leaves that machine, and before it reaches the phone.

### Windows

**A Windows PC asks your other machines.**
- aht on Windows now adds, checks and watches your Mac and Linux machines over Windows' own ssh, shows their sessions in the Sessions tab and searches them.  For that the PC needs no ssh server.
- *Check* (`aht remote check`) now groups its rows *For asking* and *For handing over*, and on a PC its fixes are Windows' own (ssh-agent, accepting a machine's key once, Remote Login on a Mac).  The guide's new *A Windows PC with your other machines* walks through the keys.
- A PC now copies its backups to one of your Mac or Linux machines after each daily backup (*Copy Now*, `aht backup --offsite`), and *Fetch Backups From…* (`aht backup --fetch-offsite`) brings backups from there to the PC.
- `aht remote add` and `aht remote check` now learn after one harmless `echo` that a machine is a Windows PC, and send it no shell script; before, they left folders named `-p` and `$HOME` in the PC's home.

**A Windows PC that answers (optional).**
- With OpenSSH Server on the PC, a Mac or Linux machine now hands a project over to the PC (`aht handover <path> --to pc`) and takes it back, watches the PC, lists its sessions and searches them.
- Such a PC also takes Keep in sync (`aht mirror <path> --on --to pc`, with the same pauses before anything is overwritten as any machine, and a name Windows cannot hold such as `aux.md` stops a sync before anything is sent), keeps another computer's backups (`offsite_backup = pc`; *Fetch Backups From…* brings them back), takes a Send Back of a project it handed over (before, only Take Back on the PC returned it), and is handed projects by another PC.
- No session starts on the PC: its tray says *shop came from mac — Continue here* (once as a notice, then in its menu until the project leaves), and Continue here opens Claude Code in a console there, in the session handed over; nothing runs until you type.
- On the PC, aht installed there answers (this version or newer); otherwise aht's own copy answers with the PC's Python 3 (`py` or `python`); with neither, *Add* stops with *install aht on pc* and makes nothing there.  aht sends a PC no shell script: one command line that cmd.exe and PowerShell read alike.
- *Check* has a PC's own rows (*aht answers there*, *Claude Code there*, *aht installed there*, *no session starts there*), and the machine lists say whether a PC answers and why not (`answers`, `answers_why`).  When Claude Code on the PC is another version, the first handover runs `claude install <version>` there.
- aht never ends a session on a PC (`--stop` does not), and `--agent`, a task's work and the night shift stay with Mac and Linux machines.  `aht remote discover` now lists Windows machines on your Tailscale network too.
- The guide's new *A Windows PC that answers* says how to set the PC up safely: key login only (`administrators_authorized_keys` for an administrator's account), `PasswordAuthentication no`, a firewall rule for Tailscale or your own network only, and no change of the network's profile.  The protocol between machines is now 3.

**Folder badges.**  aht no longer keeps a badge it had to draw without Windows' own folder icon (for example the flat ∞ folder an older aht cached).  A folder whose badge shows such a plain drawn folder gets Windows' own on its next refresh (`aht icons --refresh`, or *Refresh all badges* in the tray) or its next badge change.  aht removes older versions' cache files in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\aht\icons` the first time it makes a badge.  A folder's badge in Explorer now also changes as soon as aht changes it, even in an Explorer window that is already open: the badge file is now `.aht\aht-badge-<8 hex>.ico`, named after its picture, so Explorer draws a changed one afresh, and the old file goes.

**Removing a history** (`aht tidy --remove-history`, and *Remove…* in the Mac app's Tidy Up): on Windows a history now goes to the Recycle Bin, and only there.  When it cannot (the drive has no Recycle Bin, its bin removes files at once, or the history is bigger than the bin holds), aht changes nothing and says why; you can still delete it yourself.  A link in Claude's history folder (to a folder elsewhere) is listed but never removed: the Mac app's Tidy Up shows it as *Claude Code, a link to a folder elsewhere*, without *Remove…*.  A refused removal prints the name and why, never what it would have done.

**Choosing a folder in aht's window** (Windows and Linux): *Cancel* just closes the chooser.  On Windows you can type or paste a path into the chooser's *Folder:* field; a path with no folder behind it is reported, and nothing changes.  The Windows chooser no longer goes through PowerShell, which compiled a few lines of C# each time (a pattern antivirus tools often flag): aht shows Windows' own folder dialog itself, in a second process (`aht.exe _pick-folder`).

### Sync safety

**Keep in sync looks before it overwrites.**
- Before each sync aht compares the copy on the other machine with its list from the last sync, handover or take-back, so no clock matters.  When that copy was worked on (a file that was only touched does not count), when the sync would remove more than 200 files there or more than a quarter of at least 20, or when a first sync would go into a folder that holds something else, the sync pauses, sends nothing and gives one notice ("Keep in sync paused: api").
- The project lists the files and offers *Bring Them Here…* (Take Back on the copy: a file changed on both machines keeps both versions, then the sync runs; `aht reclaim <path> --apply`), *Replace Them…* (`aht mirror <path> --replace --apply`; theirs are set aside there), *Allow the Removals…* (`--allow-removals --apply`) or *Stop Syncing* (`--off`).
- Hand Over now stops over a changed copy too; `aht handover <path> --replace-there` sets that work aside there and goes on.  Turning a released sync back on looks first in the same way.
- The other machine notes its copies in `~/.aht/remote/copies.json`, so aht there refuses to keep such a folder in sync as well, *Keep All Projects in Sync* there leaves it out, the project there says *Copy kept in sync from mac*, and a Claude session there hears one line about it.
- In the Machines tab each machine says how many projects are kept in sync with it and how many are paused.  Names the other disk cannot hold apart (`README.md` and `readme.md`) are listed by `aht mirror --run --json` and by the dry runs of `--replace` and `--allow-removals`.
- A sync run now checks each project again right before it sends it, so a project released, handed over or switched off while the run is under way is not sent (the run lists it as *paused* or *skipped*).

**Nothing lost on the way back.**
- A file whose name changed only in case on the other machine (`readme.md` → `README.md`) now comes back on a Mac, with the old one set aside; two names that differ only in case are both kept; empty folders made there (a packed git repo's `refs`) come back too.
- Files set aside, here and on the other machine, keep the newest 5 folders and everything younger than 30 days; Claude's checkpoints and plans replaced on the other machine are now set aside too.
- A project's `.aht/handover/` keeps every hand-off that is still open and the newest 12 other summaries, handover and switch alike (before, 5 and 8, and each kind deleted the other's).  Keep in sync no longer sends that folder, and a handover never removes anything from it on the other machine.

### File copy

**aht's own file copy:** files now move between your machines without rsync.
- rsync still copies them when this machine has rsync 3, the other has rsync, and neither is Windows; otherwise aht's own copy does, over the same ssh, with nothing but python3 on the other machine.  rsync is now optional: it makes big changes faster.  `aht doctor` now lists rsync 3 as optional.
- aht's own copy sends each file in pieces of at most 1 MB, checks it when it has arrived and only then puts it in place (if that fails, the old file goes back); what it replaces or removes is set aside first, on whichever machine receives, as with rsync.  A file that only grew, such as a conversation that went on, sends just its new end.
- Against rsync it gives up two things: a big file changed in the middle is sent whole, and a big file cut off halfway starts again next time (the files that arrived whole stay).
- The new setting `handover_transfer` (`auto`, `rsync` or `aht`; Settings → Handover → *Copies files with*, in the Mac app and in aht's window) chooses, and *Check* (`aht remote check`) says which one each machine gets.

### Permissions

**The permission level follows the work.**
- When you start a session in a mode that does not ask (Claude Code's `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, Codex's full bypass) or asks less, the agent that continues the work now starts in its own equivalent: Switch, Hand Back, Pick Up → Open in, Bring Here, Hand Over and the night shift, on this machine and across machines.  *Continue Here* reopens a session in its level too.
- aht never raises the level on its own; it carries the level you chose, and restarts keep a session's own flags.  The next agent never gets more power than the session it continues: without an exact match it starts in the next stricter level (Kimi Code has no edits-only mode, so it asks), and a never-ask session inside Claude Code's sandbox goes on in Codex's sandbox (`-a never -s workspace-write`), not its full bypass.
- aht tells the level from an open session's command line (up to its first prompt, and never above what the session itself notes), Codex's `turn_context`, the permission mode Claude Code notes on each prompt, the level it started an agent in (kept on this computer; the hand-off's record in the project shows it but is not believed), or Claude Code's `defaultMode` (a project's own `.claude` settings count only up to edits mode, as in Claude Code); unknown means ask.  Only levels you set yourself raise what the next agent gets: your command line, your user or managed settings, aht's settings, or a level aht recorded on this computer.
- Every dialog and dry run says it (*Codex starts in never-ask mode, like the Claude Code session you are leaving*), and `--json` carries `perm`.
- New settings: `agent_permissions` (`follow`, a fixed level, or a cap such as `max:auto`) and `agent_permission_flags` (per agent and level, flags that replace aht's own, such as Codex's never-ask that keeps its sandbox).
- Kimi Code reads its summary in a run of its own only in never-ask mode (that run never asks and takes no level flag); below it, Kimi opens in its level and aht shows the line to paste as your first message.  A second opinion works in a throwaway copy, so Claude may edit that copy at any level while its commands follow the level; Kimi takes part only in never-ask mode, and `aht second-opinion … --dry-run` shows the levels before anything starts.

### Masking and secrets

**Keys are masked whole.** Fixes to the masking in 0.13.0 and earlier:
- A key, token or password that aht recognises in an agent's history is now masked whole, however long (up to 64 KB), and before the text is shortened, wherever aht copies text out of a history: the search index (messages, the commands, file paths and web addresses of tool calls, and session titles), handover and switch summaries, the journal, notices (also on the phone), shared session pages (also `--tools`), Tidy Up's preview, What Changed, and the notes for informed sessions, loose ends and second opinions.
- Session titles and names, tab titles and names waiting for a session's next prompt are now masked wherever aht lists them: the session board (also what other machines receive, and other machines'), loose ends, a handover's dry run and result, Take Back, What Changed, `aht undo --list`, `aht checkup` (also its `--restart` plan), `aht sessions`, `aht tab-names` (its list, `--json` and its sync plan), saved workspaces, and `aht limits`' usage-limit text.  They stay as they are only on this computer: in the Mac's session corner, the iTerm2 tab titles aht sets, aht's files about tabs in `~/.aht/run`, the tab titles of saved workspaces (restoring a layout sets them back) and `aht.log`.
- What earlier versions got wrong: they could leave part of a long key in clear (for example most of an API key after `x-api-key:`, or a long Google, Firebase or Azure ID token), could cut a text, such as a tool's command at 400 characters, in the middle of a key before masking it, masked only the first line of a private key (and masked the BEGIN line of a guide that only named one), cut a password in quotes at a `,`, `;` or closing bracket in it, took a value of capital letters and digits (a TOTP seed, say), a dotted value or one starting with `/`, `~` or `.` for a name or a path, and missed `Authorization: Bearer` tokens.
- Now also masked: values after names that contain a secret word (`DB_PASSWORD=`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=`, `SECRET_KEY=`, `JWT_SECRET=`, `client_secret`, `GITHUB_TOKEN=`, `PGPASSWORD=`, `x-api-key:`, `RAILS_MASTER_KEY=`, `APP_KEY=`, `*_PAT=`, `passphrase`, in a `.env` file or an `export` line too) and after camelCase and PascalCase names (`dbPassword`, `accessToken`, `SecretAccessKey`, `SessionToken`), but not names that say they hold something else (`TOKEN_URL`, `password_hash`, `token_type`, `max_tokens`, `accessTokenUrl`) or a page's token (`NextToken`, `nextPageToken`); a value in quotes, over the `,`, `;` and brackets in it; `Authorization:` with any scheme, and `Basic` credentials; passwords and tokens on a command line (`--password`, `--token`, `--with-token`, `--api-key` and the like, `mysql -p`, `docker login -p`, `twine -p`, `sshpass -p`, `redis-cli -a`, `curl -u user:password`), and in XML (`<password>…</password>`, `key="…Password" value="…"`); Google OAuth tokens (`ya29.…`), GitLab, SendGrid, PyPI, age, Vault, DigitalOcean, Shopify, Docker Hub and Atlassian tokens, the secret part of Slack webhook addresses and Telegram bot tokens; passwords in database addresses whatever the host (`localhost`, an IP address, a container's name such as `@db`, `[::1]`), with or without a user name, also percent-encoded or with an `@` in them, and in Go's form `user:password@tcp(…)`, with the rest of the address left readable; passwords with symbols in them (`$`, `%`, `(`, `{`, a closing bracket), masked whole; tokens followed by `...`, `</code>` or `%0A`; passwords of 12 to 16 characters that mix three kinds of character (small and capital letters, digits, symbols); and private keys from their BEGIN line to their END line (also with `>` or `#` before each line), also inside JSON (and JSON inside JSON), in Read-tool output with line numbers, encrypted keys with `Proc-Type` and `DEK-Info` lines, PGP private-key blocks, PuTTY `.ppk` files, and keys in base64 (a kubeconfig's `client-key-data`, a Kubernetes `tls.key`).
- Left alone: ordinary code that uses the words token, password, secret or auth (`token = tokenizer.encode(text)`, `password: Optional[str]`), placeholders and references to a secret store (`${DB_PASSWORD}`, `op://…`, `vault:…`), test names, paths, hashes and words, and a guide or code that names a private key's BEGIN and END lines.
- Masking is best effort: aht cannot recognise every secret, and does not try to guess at every shape a secret could have; PRIVACY.md lists the known limits (a value with no name or form it knows, one that does not look generated, a password with a quote or a space in it, a private key seen only from its middle, among others), so keep secrets out of agent chats.  On a large history, finding keys now takes about 1.5 times as long as in 0.13.0.  Journals and summaries written before stay as they were.

**The search index is rebuilt once**, by itself, at its first update after this version: an index from an earlier version could hold parts of keys, for example from long tool commands.  The old file is deleted first, so the rebuild needs no extra disk space and nothing of its old rows stays (on Windows, while a search has the file open, its tables are emptied and the file compacted instead), so `aht search --rebuild` by hand is not needed.  While an update runs, the watcher and the session-start hook no longer start more updates that would only wait for it.  A session whose history file is gone and that no history backup holds is no longer searchable after that rebuild.

**`aht secrets`** now also lists `Bearer` and `Basic` credentials, `.env` names, connection strings and the other forms above, also a name at the start of a later line of a tool's output and in JSON inside JSON (before, `aht secrets`, `--redact` and the handover's count found such a name only on the first line), so it may list more finds than before, and fewer false ones in code.  It lists a private key once, as its header, even when the history holds it twice (the Read tool's numbered copy and the file's text), and `--redact` takes out the key from its BEGIN line to its END line, and nothing around it (0.13.0 took out only the header line); a place whose removal would leave a line of the history no longer valid JSON is left as it is, and aht says so; a header with no key under it, as in a guide, is no longer listed.  A new scan then no longer finds it.  A key of a known kind is listed once, not again as *password or token*.

### Also new or fixed

- **Linux:** the watcher's systemd unit now really applies its start limit: when the watcher keeps crashing and is started 5 times within 60 seconds, systemd stops restarting it, instead of trying every 10 seconds forever.  A restart you ask for (Restart Watcher, adding or removing a watched folder, `aht roots`, `aht reload`, setup, or resuming in the tray) clears that limit first: it never stops the watcher, and it starts a stopped one again at once.  `linux/install.sh` (or `aht reload`) rewrites the unit.  Start-at-login entries now also work for folder names with a newline or tab, and when the path to Python holds a `%` they start the same Python by a path without one.
- **Linux, git folders:** the git mark is now aht's own emblem, a white disc with a dark "+", instead of the theme's link arrow, which made git folders look like links.  After the update the watcher puts it on every git folder once; `linux_git_emblem` still picks another emblem.  `aht uninstall --remove-icons` now also removes the emblem images aht drew, and `~/.local/share/icons/hicolor/icon-theme.cache` when aht's emblems were the last icons there; when other icons remain, it writes that cache again without aht's emblems.
- **New projects:** the *A new project is found* setting is gone.  aht takes on new projects as you work in them; an old config's `new_policy` and `--news` from old scripts are accepted and ignored.  A project you *Forget* now stays forgotten: the next scan does not take it on again, and setting up again lists it unticked.  It comes back when you take it on yourself: a new Claude Code session in its folder, `aht tag`, *Adopt This Mac's Projects…* or `aht adopt`, ticking it when you set up again, Tidy Up's *Reconnect* or *Choose Folder…* onto it (`aht bind`), `aht restore` into it, handing it over or keeping it in sync.  The adopt question names up to three such folders, then "and N more", in the Mac app and in the trays.
- **Options given twice** now add up: `aht setup --apply --adopt A --adopt B` takes on both, and `aht config --set backup_keep=20 --set notify_finished=false` sets both.  Before, only the last one counted.
- **Welcome and start at login:** a first setup that turns *start at login* off is now kept as your answer, in the Mac app and in aht's window, so *Getting started* marks the login step optional.
- **Attach:** `aht attach --print`, `aht attach --window` and the *open it* line after a handover gave an empty command instead of the one that opens the session over there.
- **Phone notices only encrypted:** `notify_phone` takes an ntfy server only with `https://` (`http://` only for a server on this computer: `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`); `aht config --set` refuses the rest and says why.  An `http://` address set before gets no notices, and the log and *Send a Test* say why.
- **No watcher at all:** `watcher_owner=none` now stops a running watcher on a Mac and on Linux and removes its LaunchAgent or unit, and `aht install` then sets none up.  The watcher is what relinks a project's histories as soon as you move or rename its folder; without it only Claude Code's hook relinks, when a session starts there.
- **Bring Here and Send Back** now ask for aht at protocol 3 on the project's home (the protocol at which every aht has all their operations), and say *update aht on mac first: …* when it is older.
- **Small files stay small:** the notice queues for the Mac app and the Windows tray start over after 500 notices, and the progress files of a job (`--status-file`, the Mac app's `stage-*.json`) are deleted when it ends.
- **The window's *Copy the folder when a session starts*** shows what aht really does: `aht status --json` gives `effective.checkpoint_on_start` (off by default on Windows and Linux, where the copies are real copies).

### Privacy policy

[PRIVACY.md](https://github.com/havurgiray/agent-history-tether/blob/master/PRIVACY.md) changed with this release.  It now also covers:

- **New versions:** the update check (off until you say yes; GitHub then sees your computer's address and which version you run).
- **aht's window on Windows and Linux,** served to your own browser at 127.0.0.1 only, its folder chooser, and the three iTerm2 settings *Getting started* reads.
- **Masking:** what aht masks and where, that it is best effort and its known limits, where session names and tab titles stay as they are (this computer only), what a shared page removes and leaves, and that the search index is built anew once; a handover's task and the name a handed-over session shows in Remote Control are masked before they leave.
- **aht's own files:** `machine.json` (a random id of this computer), `offsite.json`, `run/autostart.json`, `run/perm.json`, `run/claude-sandbox.json`, `run/board.json`, `run/incoming.jsonl`, `remote/copies.json`, the new handover and Keep in sync data in `registry.json`, the projects you told aht to forget, and how long set-aside files and backups on another machine are kept.
- **Claude Code's files:** what a handover reads and changes in `~/.claude.json`, and the copies aht keeps of `settings.json`.
- **Switching agents:** what aht reads of Antigravity's and Mistral Vibe's data folders and what it never reads there, a copy of Codex's `state_5.sqlite` (only to count the sessions aht cannot read), the hand-off records in a project's `.aht/handover/`, the git state a summary reads, and the lines aht's hook adds to a Claude session.
- **The permission level:** what aht reads to learn a session's level (the permission flags on its command line, Codex's `turn_context`, Claude Code's `permissionMode`, `defaultMode` and `sandbox.enabled`), and that it keeps only the level.
- **Your other machines:** when aht reads `~/.ssh/config` and Tailscale's machine list, what it asks a machine (its open sessions, every 2 minutes for one you watch, and search excerpts, masked there), that the log names your machines, the small files aht writes there to start a handover's session, and keeping a machine awake.
- **Pick Up and Leave a Note:** what aht sends to find the project there, what it reads (a masked summary and the git state) and what it writes (only new files, at most 200 KB each).
- **Keep in sync and aht's own file copy:** the file lists and checksums read from the copy there and kept here, what a paused sync records, and the temporary `.aht-partial` folder.
- **Bring Here and Send Back:** what aht reads from the project's home and writes there, and the trust it sets here.
- **Another agent on the other machine:** what aht reads from that agent's tmux window there, and that `--stop` reads its newest messages and types its quit keys.
- **A Windows PC that answers:** what aht reads and writes on such a PC, including the record that waits for *Continue here* (`~\.aht\arrivals\`), a copy kept in sync there, backups kept there and a Send Back to it.
- **Notices:** ntfy only over HTTPS, and the notice queues for the Mac app and the Windows tray, which now hold at most 500 notices.
- **On each system:** where a history you remove with `aht tidy` goes, Linux's emblem images and their icon cache, Windows' new badge file names, the files aht briefly makes to test a folder, and Kimi Code's real folder (`~/.kimi-code`).

### Unsigned builds

The app is ad-hoc signed, so macOS blocks its first launch (downloaded or Homebrew-installed alike): allow it once under System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway, or run `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/aht.app`. Windows SmartScreen shows "unknown publisher" on first run: choose *More info > Run anyway*. The checksums above let you verify what you downloaded.

Every artifact was built and smoke-tested on the matching CI runner before publishing.
